skill.name: threejs-fundamentals
skill.description: Three.js scene setup: scenes and fog, cameras, the renderer and tone mapping, the animation loop, object hierarchies, transforms, core math and cleanup, on WebGL or with WebGPU and TSL. Use when creating a scene from scratch, configuring a camera or renderer, handling resize, or arranging objects.
skill.summary: Set up, animate, and clean up Three.js scenes with WebGL or WebGPU.
skill.author: cloudai-x

content.value_statement: A Three.js scene can render incorrectly when its camera, renderer, and canvas size are out of sync. Use r186 examples to configure those pieces, animate objects, and release resources.
actual_capabilities: Set up a lit mesh, scene background, fog, and a browser animation loop.
Configure perspective, orthographic, array, and cube cameras, including resize and viewport handling.
Tune WebGL renderer pixel ratio, tone mapping, exposure, and shadows.
Organize objects into groups and use local transforms, world transforms, and visibility layers.
Initialize WebGPURenderer, use node materials, and check whether its WebGL 2 fallback is active.
Release unused geometry, materials, and textures, and use renderer counters to inspect draw calls and resource counts.
limitations: The examples target Three.js r186. Check API differences before adapting them to another release.
The optional browser import maps depend on jsDelivr when the browser imports a mapped module.
The WebGPU example does not guarantee WebGPU support on a given browser or device.
The guide covers scene fundamentals, not full workflows for model loading, skeletal animation, or post-processing.

use_cases.title: Create a first animated scene
use_cases.description: Set up a lit cube with a perspective camera and keep it correctly framed when the window resizes.

use_cases.title: Clean up an embedded 3D view
use_cases.description: Stop the animation loop and release renderer resources when removing a 3D view without disposing of assets still shared by other meshes.

use_cases.title: Compare WebGPU and its fallback
use_cases.description: Initialize a WebGPU scene with a node material and check how it runs on the WebGL 2 fallback.

prompt_templates.title: Start with a rotating cube
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: create a first Three.js scene.
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a minimal Three.js r186 scene with a lit cube, a perspective camera, and WebGLRenderer. Rotate the cube using elapsed frame time and update the camera and renderer when the window resizes.

prompt_templates.title: Keep an orthographic view proportional
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: fix stretching in a resizable canvas.
prompt_templates.prompt: Adapt my orthographic camera to a resizable canvas. Keep the visible world height fixed, recalculate the horizontal bounds from the canvas aspect ratio, and update the projection matrix.

prompt_templates.title: Plan resource cleanup
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: remove a scene with shared assets.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my Three.js scene cleanup. Show how to stop the loop, disconnect the timer, and dispose of GPU resources only after their last use.

prompt_templates.title: Migrate a scene to WebGPU
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: adapt a WebGL scene to WebGPURenderer.
prompt_templates.prompt: Adapt my Three.js r186 scene to WebGPURenderer with a node material. Show where to await renderer initialization and how to verify the WebGL 2 fallback.

output_examples.input: Why does my scene stretch after I resize the window?
output_examples.output: The renderer changed size, but the perspective camera still uses the old aspect ratio. Set the new aspect ratio, refresh the projection matrix, and resize the renderer to match the canvas.

output_examples.input: What should I release when I close a 3D view?
output_examples.output: Stop the animation loop and disconnect the timer. Remove the meshes and release geometries, materials, and textures only when no other mesh uses them. Dispose of the renderer when you no longer need it.

output_examples.input: How do I avoid drawing before WebGPURenderer is ready?
output_examples.output: Await renderer initialization before configuring or rendering the scene. After initialization, check which backend is active and register the animation loop.

best_practices: Update the camera projection whenever its aspect ratio or orthographic bounds change.
Cap the renderer pixel ratio where high-density displays make rendering too expensive.
Use a locked dependency version and bundle it locally for deployments that should not rely on a public CDN.
anti_patterns: Render with WebGPURenderer before initialization finishes.
Use fractional values for ArrayCamera viewport dimensions under WebGLRenderer instead of drawing-buffer pixels.
Dispose of shared materials or textures while another mesh still uses them.

faq.question: Which Three.js release does the guide target?
faq.answer: The examples target r186. Check your installed release before using the migration advice.

faq.question: Can I use the examples without a bundler?
faq.answer: Yes. The guide provides browser import maps for WebGL and WebGPU, both pinned to Three.js 0.186.0 on jsDelivr.

faq.question: Does it cover both perspective and orthographic cameras?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers their projection settings and resize handling, plus ArrayCamera for multiple views and CubeCamera for reflections.

faq.question: What if the browser does not support WebGPU?
faq.answer: WebGPURenderer can fall back to WebGL 2. Check the active backend after initialization and test your scene on the target browser.

faq.question: How does the animation loop handle a hidden tab?
faq.answer: The examples connect a Three.js Timer to the document. This prevents a large time step when the tab becomes visible again.

faq.question: Does removing a mesh release its GPU resources?
faq.answer: No. Dispose of unused geometry, materials, and textures separately, and keep any resources still used by other objects.
